title: Brooklyn man sues, saying he warned of cracks before deadly building collapse
summary:
Dengane Omari Jack filed a lawsuit against his landlord and multiple construction companies

A Brooklyn man who lost his home in the…

blocks.text: A Brooklyn man who lost his home in the building collapse that killed eight people last week has said he raised concerns about visible cracks in the brickwork weeks before the disaster.

Dengane Omari Jack, 48, made the allegations in a lawsuit filed against his landlord and multiple construction companies after the apartment building on Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a neighboring construction site on 11 November.
Investigators are still working to establish the cause of the collapse, which claimed the lives of two children, and left several others injured.

According to the court filing, Jack had spotted cracks near the entrance of the building in October and photographed the damage before sending the pictures to his landlord. But rather than being assured that the problem would be addressed, Jack claims his concerns were dismissed.
“Plaintiff was falsely told, in substance, that the condition was not the landlord’s fault or could not be fixed,” the lawsuit said.
The collapsed apartment building stood beside an active construction site where another structure had already been demolished and excavation work was underway for a new residential development.

The lawsuit seeks to hold the landlord and construction companies connected to both properties accountable for allegedly neglecting to act on the structural concerns Jack reported before the deadly collapse.

The defendants “failed to arrange a timely and adequate structural investigation, obtain necessary protection or repairs, or take appropriate steps in response to the reported condition and the ongoing adjoining excavation”, the lawsuit said.
The former tenant is suing for reimbursement for rent he previously paid, a replacement apartment and additional financial compensation.

Jack, who works as a musician and DJ, told the New York Post he had occupied a top-floor apartment in the building for five years. He escaped the disaster because he was working at a school at the time the structure came crashing down.

An extensive music collection, which Jack had spent decades assembling, was lost in the disaster. Speaking to Gothamist, he said thousands of albums collected over about 30 years now lay beneath the rubble, with some dating back to when he emigrated to the US from St Vincent and the Grenadines as a teenager. Jack estimated the collection’s value at more than $100,000.

Built in 1930, the Brooklyn building was 96-years-old when it crumbled. Records from New York City’s department of housing, preservation, and development show the property had accumulated 98 violations dating back to 1972.

Eleven of those violations were issued within the past year, including one involving “unsafe electrical wiring” and another directing the property owner to “provide an adequate supply of water for the wet sprinkler and/or standpipe.”

The city’s Department of Buildings and law enforcement authorities have launched an investigation into the incident, focused on both the condition of the destroyed apartment building and the construction activity taking place next door.
